annotations.text: The chosen look: Brutal, calmer, on the Diary structure. This is what the SwiftUI port is built from. Tokens: paper #F3F0E8 / ink #1C1A17 / lime #C6F135 / hairline #DED9CE; dark is ink on #111111 with the same lime. 1.5px borders, 6px radius, hard 2px shadows only on things you can press. Type is SF Pro in the app; Space Grotesk here is the stand-in.

Today screen, three directions. All three fix the same two things: the bin-week card stops being a hero block and becomes a line of context, and the section links stop being a list at the bottom. The agenda loses its boxed buckets in every option. Dark theme only for now, matching the screenshot. Amounts on the section tiles ($1,240/mo, $3,410 FY26) are sample figures.

A · Tabs
Navigation-first. A native tab bar makes Bins, Tasks, Bills and Receipts one tap from anywhere; Diagnostics moves behind the gear. Bin week is a single tinted strip that always shows the next bin night.

For: zero learning curve, the most iOS-native answer, keeps the calm.
Against: the least exciting of the three, the tab bar costs 83pt of every screen, and the live stats the old link list carried are gone.

B · Diary (chosen)
Editorial. The date is the title, then one written sentence summarises the day. Sections sit under it as a scrolling shelf, each carrying its live number. The agenda runs down a single timeline rail with serif day headings.

For: leans hardest into the notebook brand, and the sentence makes the screen feel alive.
Against: the summary has to read well in every state (empty, overdue, ten bills), and a horizontal shelf is easy to miss.

C · Tiles
At a glance. Four equal tiles, one per section, each showing the thing you'd open it to find out. The tile is the link, so navigation and information are the same object. Below, one flat list in date order with a day gutter.

For: answers everything in one glance, nothing feels like an afterthought.
Against: densest option and the closest to the 'productivity dashboard' the brief warns against. Tiles need good empty states.

Looks explored on the Diary skeleton before choosing. The brand brief was set aside on purpose: different fonts, palettes and surfaces in each. Same content in all so only the look changes. The chosen one, Brutal calmer, now lives on the Today page.

Quiet
Warm minimalism, the 'quiet luxury' end of the trend. Cream paper, one bronze accent, Instrument Serif at display size, no cards and no icons anywhere. The summary sentence is the whole header.

Best at: calm and stillness. Weak at: dense weeks; there is nowhere for a fifth bin or an overdue badge to go.

Acid
Monochrome dark with one acid accent, the current developer-tool look. Geist and Geist Mono, hairlines, a time column, numbers set in mono. Lime is used exactly twice.

Best at: precision, feels engineered. Weak at: warmth; it can read cold for a home app.

Swiss
Flat design taken to its typographic root. Black on white, a giant date numeral, rules instead of cards, one signal red. Archivo plus IBM Plex Mono.

Best at: hierarchy and print-like clarity. Weak at: friendliness; it is confident rather than cosy.

Liquid Glass
Apple's current system language: translucent panels with blur, a specular top edge and soft light blobs behind. Bin dots glow.

Best at: feeling native on iOS 26 and genuinely lively. Weak at: minimalism; the backdrop does a lot of talking, and legibility depends on what is behind the glass.

Soft
Neumorphism. One pale surface everywhere; elements are pressed out of it or into it with paired shadows. Manrope, one teal accent.

Best at: tactile, calm, everything feels like one material. Weak at: contrast; controls are subtle enough to miss, and it does not translate to dark mode well.

Brutal
Neo-brutalism at full volume. Two-pixel black borders, hard offset shadows, square bin swatches, one lime fill. Space Grotesk. The calmer version of this is the one that was chosen.

Brutal, colour-block
The most common form of the trend: every block gets its own flat pastel, black borders and offset shadows hold it together. Header on lime, one colour per section, so colour is navigation.

Loudest of the set. Best at joy and wayfinding; worst at calm.

Brutal, mono
Zine brutalism. Pure black and white, 3px borders, 6px shadows, Archivo Black for the date and every number, solid black day bars. The only colour is the bin lids.

Most minimal of the brutalist set. Reads as printed, not designed.

Brutal, sticker
The playful branch: pills instead of boxes, slightly rotated day tags like stuck-on labels, dashed rules, a dot-grid paper behind. Section stats become a wrapping row of sticker chips instead of tiles.

Friendliest brutalism; the rotation is the risk, it can tip into novelty.

Brutal, grid
Raw-HTML brutalism. One continuous table: every cell bordered, no gaps, no shadows, Space Mono for labels and times, lime only on the Tonight row. Section stats are four tight columns.

Densest and most honest. Best on data; hardest for small type.

The section lists in the chosen look, replacing the stock iOS grouped lists. Same anatomy as Today: a bordered box per section, an uppercase label above it, hairline rules between rows, 17pt Space Grotesk titles with a 12pt SF Pro detail line. Rows are 56pt on two lines. The plus button becomes a small lime block. Swipe actions keep the ink border and use the alert red for delete. Names and amounts are sample data.

Bills
The monthly figure sits in its own box with the Reports link as a row inside it, so the headline and where it leads are one object. Per-row: name with the 'varies' tag, cadence and who pays, and the monthly equivalent on the right with a quiet /mo. Paused bills go grey with a bordered tag.

Tasks
Same tick box as Today, hanging in the left gutter so the title column lines up with Bills. Overdue is a red label and red detail, with a bordered '2 missed' tag when one tap won't clear it. Settled tasks show a lime ticked box. The undo banner floats above the list with a slightly deeper shadow, since it's the one thing that moves.

The bill editor, the pattern every other form follows. Fields become two-line rows: a small uppercase label over the value in 17pt, so a filled form reads as a document rather than a settings screen. New controls here: a bordered toggle with a lime track and a square knob, a stepper as two shadowed squares, weekday chips as a 7-across grid, and category suggestions as bordered pills. Delete is the one red thing, outlined rather than filled so it is not the loudest object on screen.

One addition worth a look: the pale-lime box after the schedule. The old editor buried the normalisation in a footer sentence. Since the whole point of a bill is what it costs a month, it gets to be a figure. Date and time stay native pickers behind those two bordered chips, because a custom date picker is a lot of surface for little gain.

Two dark-mode problems, one root cause. In dark mode surface and background are both #111111, so a box is nothing but its border and the only filled shapes are the ones we paint in ink. That makes the cream day band the loudest thing on the screen, and it turns the hard shadow into a glow, because a shadow lighter than its surface is backwards. Options for each are stacked here against the current build, all on the Blossom accent.

Organising the Tasks screen. Three things are true of the current one: it is ordered by when each task was created, which means nothing to anyone; a one-off reminder and a standing commitment look identical although they behave nothing alike; and the Done section is already reminders-only by accident, because isFinished can only ever be true for a one-off. All three options fix the sort and surface the kind. Sample data, lime accent.

A · Two sections
One scroll. Anything overdue floats to the top whatever it is, then Reminders, then Recurring sorted by what is next, with paused ones sunk to the bottom.

For: no new chrome, everything visible at once, and the header line says the state in words.
Against: with twenty recurring tasks the reminders get pushed off screen.

B · Two tabs
A segmented control splits the screen into Recurring and Reminders, each with its own grouping. Recurring groups by horizon — this week, this month, later — which is the useful cut once a list gets long.

For: scales, and each tab can be organised on its own terms.
Against: hides half the screen behind a tap, and the count badges have to work hard to say what is on the other side.

C · By cadence
Grouped by how often: weekly, monthly, every few months, one-offs. Answers what the household has standing rather than what is next.

For: the best library view, and it makes gaps obvious — nothing yearly, no quarterly check.
Against: overdue has to be lifted into a banner or it hides inside a group, and it is the least useful cut when you just want to tick something off.

Honest scorekeeping instead of streaks. Every completion already records the due date and the tick, so the app has been keeping this record since Phase 2 and has never shown it. A rolling rate degrades gracefully: one bad week barely moves 23 of 28, where a streak would reset to zero and make the app a place you avoid. Three squares carry the whole language — filled is on time, split is late, red outline is missed. Sample data.

A · On the row
Each recurring task carries a strip of its last several occurrences, oldest on the left, with the household rate in the section header.

For: the record sits next to the thing it describes, so a task that keeps slipping is obvious while you are looking at it. No new screen.
Against: the Tasks screen gets denser, and you only see it when you go to Tasks.

B · On Today
A Kept up block above the agenda: the rate, every occurrence as a square, and one line naming whatever is slipping.

For: it is on the screen you already open, which is the whole point — you cannot ignore a record you see daily.
Against: Today is the calm screen, and this is the first thing on it that is about you rather than about the day.

C · Own screen
A Kept up screen behind Tasks: the headline rate, a meter per task worst-first, and a financial-year tally including the receipts figure.

For: room to be useful — it can name the task that is slipping and suggest the schedule is wrong rather than you. The FY tally is the honest score, since receipts turn into money at tax time.
Against: a screen nobody visits changes no behaviour. Needs A or B to pull you into it.
